content:
Good news. Here's an employment law update where nothing has changed yet  🎉 


The governments consultation on workplace monitoring technology closed at 11:59pm on 30 September, and its now going through the responses. 

Here's what was on the table. 

Option A: a statutory Code of Practice. It wouldn't create new duties, but tribunals would take it into account. If you unreasonably failed to follow it, they could adjust compensation by up to 25% in an unfair dismissal or discrimination claim. 

Option B: a legal duty to consult and negotiate with unions, or elected reps where theres no union, before you bring monitoring tech in. With a view to agreement. That one would need primary legislation, so don't hold your breath. 

Option C: guidance. No statutory footing at all. The government also says doing nothing is a legitimate outcome if the evidence doesn't show a problem. 

Bold, given the year we've had. 

Monitoring covers more than you'd think. Door entry systems, vehicle trackers, call recording, keystroke logging, software that scores performance. If it collects information about your staff, its probably in scope. 

In the meantime, UK GDPR hasnt gone anywhere. Anything intrusive already needs a DPIA. 

Have you done yours? Asking for a friend. The friend is the Information Commission. 

Full legal update on The HR Vault here: https://lnkd.in/gGYG_nVY

content:
Settlement agreements are about to get more complicated. Again.  🫠 


From 2027, any clause in an agreement between an employer and a worker will be void to the extent that it stops the worker speaking about harassment or discrimination, or about how the employer responded to it.

Settlement agreements. Employment contracts. Anything else they sign. 

It covers all harassment under the Equality Act (not just sexual harassment), discrimination on any protected ground, and harassment by clients and customers as well as colleagues. 

There is a route to a valid NDA. Its called an excepted agreement, and the government is still deciding what one needs to look like. 

The proposals so far: written advice from a named, insured independent adviser. The worker confirming in writing that they want the confidentiality. Then a 14 day cooling off period in which they can withdraw. 

Because what every settlement negotiation was missing was a fortnight of not knowing whether its settled  😭 

And even with all that in place, they'd still be able to talk to close family, a lawyer, a doctor or a regulator. 

In English: the standard confidentiality clause in your settlement template needs splitting in two, and the process will need a review.

The good news is that it wont apply to agreements signed before it comes into force. 

The less good news is that we don't know when that is yet. 

I've put together an article on The HR Vault about this and you can read it here: https://lnkd.in/g5xzsc8S

I'll be updating the Vault templates the day the regulations appear. I've pencilled it in for 2027. Lightly.
